# Microbes and their hosts

> *Most people carry potential pathogens without harm, yet the same organism can make one person ill
> and leave another well. When illness does follow, we need to know how much of the damage comes from
> the microbe and how much from the host's own response.*

## Four terms that are often confused {#sec-host-words}

The vocabulary of tissue injury comes from general pathology. Microbiology adds terms that students
often use interchangeably, although they describe different states.

| Term | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Contamination | Microbes are present on a surface but not multiplying | Bacteria on an unwashed hand |
| Colonisation | Microbes live and multiply at a site without causing damage | *Staphylococcus aureus* in the nose of a healthy person |
| Infection | Microbes multiply in tissue, and the host responds | Bacteria multiplying in a wound, with local inflammation |
| Disease | The host is damaged enough to produce signs and symptoms | Fever, pain and swelling from that wound |

Infection does not always lead to disease. In one Singapore study, 42 of 245 healthy children
attending childcare centres (17.1%) had enterovirus in their saliva with no symptoms of hand, foot and
mouth disease at the time of sampling [@min2021hfmd]. A person who harbours and can transmit an
organism without being ill is a **carrier**.

## The microbiota {#sec-host-microbiota}

The **microbiota** is the community of microbes that normally lives on and in the body: in the colon,
the mouth, the skin, the upper airway and the vagina. Most of these organisms are **commensals**,
which live on a host without harming it. The composition of the microbiota differs between sites
because each site offers different conditions: stomach acid, the dryness and salt of skin, and the
near-absence of oxygen in the colon each select for different organisms.

Resident microbes contribute to defence and to nutrition in several ways:

- They occupy attachment sites and consume nutrients that incoming organisms would need, a protection
  called **colonisation resistance**.
- Some produce substances that inhibit competitors.
- Their presence helps the immune system develop and stay regulated.
- Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre the host cannot digest, and synthesise vitamin K and several B
  vitamins.

Disturbing the community removes this protection. A course of antibacterial treatment, for example,
can allow *Clostridioides difficile*, which tolerates the disturbance, to multiply in the colon and
cause diarrhoea. Vaginal candidiasis after antibacterial treatment follows the same logic.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "microbes are germs, and germs are harmful"
Children as young as seven describe microorganisms as essentially harmful [@byrne2011children], and
the idea persists into adult life. Pathogens are in fact a small minority, and many common bacterial
infections, such as urinary tract infections and skin abscesses, are caused by organisms that also
live on people harmlessly. What usually changes is the site the organism reaches, or the state of the
host.
:::

## When a resident becomes a problem {#sec-host-opportunism}

**Virulence** is the degree to which an organism can cause disease. An **opportunistic pathogen** is an
organism of low virulence that causes disease when the host's defences are impaired, or when it reaches
a site it does not normally occupy. It usually gets that opportunity in one of these ways:

1. A barrier is breached: skin is cut, a catheter crosses it, or surgery opens the bowel so that gut
   organisms reach the peritoneal cavity.
2. Defences are weakened: **neutropenia** (a low neutrophil count) after chemotherapy, impaired
   cell-mediated immunity in advanced HIV infection, or impaired neutrophil function in diabetes.
3. The microbiota is disturbed, as described above.

A **primary** (or strict) **pathogen**, by contrast, causes disease in people with normal defences:
*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Salmonella* Typhi and influenza virus do not need a weakened host.
Because the boundary is not sharp, a more useful question is what it takes, in a given host, for an
organism to cause damage.

## Where the damage comes from {#sec-host-drf}

The **damage-response framework** of Casadevall and Pirofski answers that question
[@casadevall2003damage]. It holds that disease is defined by host damage, and that damage can come
from the microbe, from the host's response, or from both. If we plot damage against the strength of
the host response, different organisms give differently shaped curves.

<div data-island="damage-response" data-src="/diagrams/damage-response.yml"></div>

On the right-hand side of these curves, damage rises as the immune response grows stronger. In **toxic
shock syndrome**, a **superantigen**, a toxin that activates a large fraction of T cells at once,
triggers cytokine release that causes **hypotension** (abnormally low blood pressure) and shock. In
**rheumatic fever**, antibodies raised against *Streptococcus pyogenes* cross-react with heart tissue
weeks after the infection has cleared. In tuberculosis, much of the destruction of lung tissue is the
work of the immune response to bacteria it cannot eliminate. We return to the first two in
[*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd).

We met the same point about inflammation in general pathology: inflammation clears an infection but
damages tissue when it is excessive or prolonged.

## Host factors {#sec-host-factors}

When two people meet the same organism and only one becomes ill, the reasons usually lie with the
host. Casadevall and Pirofski group them under the mnemonic **MISTEACHING**: Microbiota, Inoculum,
Sex, Temperature, Environment, Age, Chance, History of exposure, Immunity, Nutrition and Genetics
[@casadevall2018misteaching].

Inoculum and immunity need detail now. The **inoculum**, the number of organisms received, affects
both whether disease follows and how quickly it begins; for some organisms ten to a hundred cells are
enough, while for others a million or more must be swallowed. Immunity includes the specific
immunity left by earlier exposure or vaccination and the general competence of the defences. Each
gap in the defences exposes a person to particular organisms:

- Neutropenia, to bacterial and fungal infection.
- Impaired cell-mediated immunity, to intracellular organisms such as *M. tuberculosis*.
- The absence of a functioning spleen, **asplenia**, to encapsulated bacteria such as
  *Streptococcus pneumoniae*.

Other conditions shift the balance too. Diabetes is the clearest local example. Among patients in
Singapore with **melioidosis**, infection with the soil bacterium *Burkholderia pseudomallei*, 56.7% had
diabetes between 2003 and 2014, against 19.3% of the general population of similar age
[@pang2018melioidosis].

## What a microbe has to do {#sec-host-steps}

To cause an infection, a microbe has to complete a sequence of steps. Anything it uses to complete
them is a **virulence factor**: a product or structure that helps it infect or damage a host. The
steps are:

1. Reach a surface and attach to it.
2. Invade beyond the surface, or stay on it and act from there.
3. Evade host defences long enough to multiply.
4. Obtain nutrients, iron in particular, which the host keeps bound to proteins.
5. Damage the host, directly or through the response it provokes.

Attachment explains **tropism**, the range of tissues or cells an organism can occupy. A microbe can
settle only where it finds the molecule it binds. This is why influenza virus infects cells lining the
airway and not skin, and why strains of *Escherichia coli* that bind receptors in the urinary tract
cause urinary tract infection.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/pathogenesis-sorter.yml"></div>

## Two meanings of "toxin" {#sec-host-toxins}

Students meet two things called toxins and often merge them, although they differ in almost every
respect.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-exotoxin-endotoxin.yml"></div>

Protein **exotoxins** can be inactivated and used as **toxoid** vaccines, which is how tetanus and
diphtheria are prevented. Lipopolysaccharide cannot, and the inflammation it drives causes much of the
septic shock in severe Gram-negative infection.

## The time course of infection {#sec-host-courses}

Infections differ in how they unfold over time, and the pattern often follows from the organism's
strategy.

| Pattern | What happens | Typical strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | Rapid onset and a short course | Rapid multiplication and transmission before an immune response develops |
| Latent | The organism persists silently and can reactivate | Survival inside cells, or in a site the immune response reaches poorly |
| Chronic | Infection and inflammation continue for months or years | Resistance to clearance; damage accumulates from the ongoing response |

Latency explains reactivation. Varicella-zoster virus persists in sensory ganglia after chickenpox and
can return as shingles decades later, and latent tuberculosis can reactivate when immunity falls.

## Applying these ideas in Part II {#sec-host-close}

For each organism in Part II, we ask how it damages the host: by destroying cells, by toxins, by
provoking a damaging inflammatory response, or by a combination. We then place it on the
damage-response curve. If most of the damage comes from the host's response, a weakened host may
show less visible disease, and removing the organism alone may not stop the damage.
